synopsis: Across the booklet, nuisance interventions are identified as the main documented reason mining proximity systems were disabled; bypasses, overrides, tag removal and altered zones can ultimately remove protection when needed [f116, f6306, f11764]. Direct examples include a Caterpillar 793B audible alarm found switched off after shifts and a June 2017 underground fatality involving a worker with 87 prior emergency-stop override activations; however, the alarm observation was partly anecdotal, and the research separately reports finding no field data on disabling collision mitigation systems [f3012, f3283, f11802, f5840]. ISO 16001:2017 prohibits single-action disablement, while MOSH forbids routine override use and requires monitored, abuse-resistant overrides limited to under five minutes and under 10 km/h [f2068, f2413, f2922, f5839]. Deactivation is nevertheless required in some operating conditions: Komatsu specifies switching off stop control during trailer loading because rapid stops can destabilize the machine, and wheel-loader guidance also lists slopes, slippery or soft ground and suspended loads [f1241, f10420]. On-road findings should not be treated as a uniform predictor of off-road behavior: an 18% false-alarm rate was associated with ignoring or abandoning warnings, whereas simulator studies with 20–33% false alarms still shortened brake reactions, and another finding reports 93% of drivers leaving automatic braking enabled [f3020, f3038]. Validation therefore needs to address override behavior and nuisance-induced disengagement, not just detection and stopping distance, with documented deactivation rules; whether configuration-based disabling is permissible in some markets, and its effect on the EU safety case, remains unresolved [f577, f1986, f10731, f2953].
